steps.label: Do Now: Notation (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Notation (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does prefix need no brackets?Show the answer

Each operator comes just before its two operands, so the order of the work is already fixed.

From the Prefix, Infix and Postfix lesson.

Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: prefix and postfix

steps.text: A similar prefix question: find an operator with two numbers straight after it.
Work it out and put the answer in its place: * 2 3 is 6.
A similar postfix question: a * (b - c) + d. First put brackets round every operation.
Start inside: b - c becomes b c -. Then a times that becomes a b c - *.
Last, add d: the + goes after both of its operands.
steps.visual: a b c - * d +

steps.text: Now do your two questions the same way.
steps.visual: find → work out → replace → repeat

steps.label: Do Now: Bit Strings (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Bit Strings (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a shift keep the string the same length?Show the answer

Bits fall off one end and the same number of zeros come in at the other end.

From the Bit-String Flicking lesson. Write all 5 bits.

Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: bit strings

steps.text: A similar question: RSHIFT-1 11100 XOR 01100. Shifts go first.
RSHIFT-1 moves every bit one place right. The last bit is lost and a 0 comes in on the left.
Now XOR, bit by bit: 1 where the bits are different.
Another: NOT 01110 AND LCIRC-1 11001. NOT and the circulate go before AND.
LCIRC-1 moves the bits left, and the bit that falls off comes back on the right. Then AND: 1 only where both are 1.
Now do your two questions the same way: NOT, shifts and circulates first, then AND, XOR, OR.
steps.visual: NOT, SHIFT, CIRC → AND → XOR → OR

steps.label: Contest Day
steps.content:
ACSL Junior Contest 2

Contest Day

Competition

  • Today: how the contest works, how to write answers that score, a mock contest against the clock, and the programming problem.
  • Every time, ask why: why would that answer score, or not score?
Think → Pair → ShareWhy practise a whole contest, not just one topic at a time?Show the answer

On the day the topics are mixed. You have to switch between them quickly and manage your time.

steps.label: How the Contest Works
steps.content:
How the Contest Works

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does each short question ask for only one answer, with no working?Show the answer

Answers can be checked quickly and fairly. The working is for you: it is how you get the answer right.

QuestionUsual topic
1Prefix, Infix and Postfix
2Prefix, Infix and Postfix
3Bit-String Flicking
4Bit-String Flicking
5What Does This Program Do?
  • Part 1: five short questions. Each answer is one value or one expression.
  • Part 2: a programming problem. Your program reads test input and prints the answers.
  • The program is run on test inputs. Each output that matches scores.
  • Your teacher tells you the time for each part.

steps.label: Compare: Answers That Score
steps.content:
Compare: Answers That Score

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is 110 not a good answer when the question works with 5-bit strings?Show the answer

The strings keep their length. 110 hides the two zeros at the front, so it does not show the full answer: write 00110.

Answer typeScoresDoes not score
bit string00110110
find every x1*0*110001 (only one of them)
postfixa b + c *a + b c * (still infix order)
program output25.525 (/ keeps the decimal part)
  • Give the answer in the form the question asks for.
  • Write every bit. Use * for a bit that can be 0 or 1.
  • Read it back: does it answer the question that was asked?

steps.label: Check: Which Answer Scores?
steps.content:
Check: Which Answer Scores?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy must you check whether a question says prefix or postfix before you answer?Show the answer

They put the operators in opposite places. A correct prefix answer to a postfix question scores nothing.

Choose the answer that scores.

items.prompt: x is a 5-bit string. Which answer shows every x that makes x AND 11000 = 10000 true?
items.explain: AND with 11000 keeps only the first two bits, so they must be 1 and 0. The last three bits are hidden by the 0s: each can be anything.

items.prompt: Which is the postfix form of a + b * c?
items.explain: * goes first, so b * c becomes b c *. Then a plus that: a b c * +.

steps.label: Tips for Each Question Type
steps.content:
Tips for Each Question Type

Think → Pair → ShareWhy leave no question blank, even when you are unsure?Show the answer

An answer you are unsure of can still be right. A blank can never score.

QuestionHow to get it right
Prefix, infix, postfixBracket every operation first. Evaluate with a stack, or find an operator with two numbers next to it.
Bit stringsNOT, shifts and circulates first, then AND, XOR, OR. Write each step as a new 5-bit string.
Find every xWork one bit at a time. Check your answer by putting a value of x back in.
ProgramsSay what each loop does in words. Trace a few turns. Spot the pattern.
  • Check each answer a second way if there is time.

steps.label: Activity 1: Mock Contest
steps.content:
Activity 1: Mock Contest

Think → Pair → ShareWhy practise against a clock?Show the answer

On the day, time runs out. Practising with a clock shows you which questions take you too long.

Five questions, 15 minutes. Press Start the clock when your teacher says. Nothing is marked until you hand in.

steps.label: The Programming Problem
steps.content:
The Programming Problem

Think → Pair → ShareWhy test your program with your own inputs, not just the sample?Show the answer

The program is marked on inputs you have not seen. Your own inputs, with ties and short words, find the bugs first.

line = input()
words = line.split()
print(len(words))
print(len(words[0]))

Input: Cats sleep a lot
Output: 4, then 4

  • Read the input with input().
  • Print the answers in order, one per line.
  • Print only the answer: no labels, no extra lines.
  • Test with the sample, then with inputs you make up.

steps.label: Compare: Output That Matches
steps.content:
Compare: Output That Matches

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does Words: 4 score nothing when the answer is 4?Show the answer

The output is checked line by line against the expected output. Words: 4 is not the same text as 4.

ExpectedPrintedResult
44matches
4Words: 4no match: extra text
44.0no match: a decimal, not a whole number
sleepSleepno match: capital letter
  • Match the expected output exactly.
  • Use int() or whole-number maths when the answer is a whole number.

steps.label: Activity 2: Word Stats
steps.content:
Activity 2: Word Stats

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the problem say what to do when two words tie?Show the answer

Without a rule, two different programs could both be right. The rule means there is only one correct output.

Write the program in Python. Run it on the sample, then Submit: it is tested on four more inputs you cannot see. Aim for 25 out of 25.

steps.label: More Programming Problems
steps.content:
More Programming Problems

Think → Pair → ShareWhy practise more than one problem?Show the answer

Each problem needs different Python: counting, comparing, building new strings. More problems means fewer surprises.

Contest Code has more problems in the same style: Number Line and Code Words. Each is tested on the sample and four hidden inputs.

  • Finished Word Stats? Try Number Line next.
  • Then try the official sample problem: ACSL Junior Contest 2 programming problem (PDF).

steps.content:

The sample is written by ACSL, so it shows exactly how real questions look.

Try the sample contest on paper, under the clock. Then check it together.

steps.label: Plenary: Mock Contest Drill
steps.content:
Plenary: Mock Contest Drill

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the drill bring back the kinds you got wrong?Show the answer

Mastery means getting each kind right three times in a row. The kinds you miss come back until you have them.

Five card slots, like the contest: two notation, two bit strings, one program. Every card is new each time. Choose Quiz and 5 questions for another mock. Your progress is saved.

acc_do_now.feedback: Find an operator with two numbers straight after it. Work it out, put the answer in its place, and repeat.
Bracket every operation first. Then move each operator after its two operands, from the inside out.

acc_do_now_2.feedback: Shift first: two places left, zeros come in on the right. Then OR.
Work out NOT and RCIRC-1 first. Then AND, bit by bit.
